utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We call the case, please, Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. Good morning, Your Honours. This is the Case Number IT-99-36-T, the Prosecutor versus Radislav Brdjanin.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Brdjanin, good morning to you. Can you follow in a language that you can understand?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Honours. Yes, I can do that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Appearances for the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Julian Nicholls with Denise Gustin.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. For the Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honour. John Ackerman with Aleksandar Vujic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Thank you. Any preliminaries? Nothing? Yes, Mr. Nicholls.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Not really. Three very small points. First of all, I wonder if we know when my deadline to stop is so that I can plan --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Preferably at 11.30. Preferably, because they want me -- let's go into private session for a while because I don't think this is for public consumption.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: With regard to the law of the Federal Republic and the law of Republika Srpska on -- which could reflect on command responsibility --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I don't plan to go into that, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Because I don't think we ought to have lectures from anybody on that, to be frank with you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: The second question for Your Honours is: Should I reserve time for questions from Your Honours because you may wish to ask questions before we close our --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I personally have already expressed myself. I allow expert witnesses to come over because I know that the system allows it. I come from a jurisdiction where we don't allow expert witnesses, and my idea of them is not that high. I'm telling you straight and plain. I know -- I can see the utility of the system, but frankly, I prefer to appoint my own expert.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Another point, Your Honour. I think it has been cleared up, but I would ask that I be allowed to communicate with Mr. Brown before his cross, obviously not talking about anything to do with his testimony, the report, or his cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yeah. It would be exactly the same as we did with the previous witness. You are professional people and you are trusted as such.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: The very last point, Your Honour, which is not a big point, just for the record, the document in footnote 451 about which there was some confusion yesterday, that is, in fact, part of Exhibit P717. We compared the B/C/S originals yesterday in both, so --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: My secretary told me so this morning, because I asked her to check, too. And you are correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: So we did assign that as 2423 yesterday, but it can either be left --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Leave it as it is now because you would confuse Mr. Ackerman --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Your Honours, excuse me, but could this exchange be slowed down because it is difficult for interpreters to follow.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So please allow no time for questions from the Bench. If any at all, we'll put those after the cross-examination. Ms. Gustin, witnesses are being asked by my colleagues to have confirmation for the witnesses next week. Ms. Gustin, 7.57 first for cross-examination; 7.89 to follow; 7.279; and then last but not least, 7.22 cross-examination only.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Your Honour, can I confirm that after the break, and I'll check --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: In the meantime, please work out on a complete list of witnesses until the 1st of August because my staff has required it. And I am not in a position to give it to them because I don't know who is coming and when. So please if you can help me there. Mr. Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, the last witness scheduled for next week is a bit ify ---

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Is a bit --

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Because it depends on -- as you recall that involves the book that was sent to CLSS for translation. We asked them to have it back to us by the 15th of July, and I don't know if they are going to be able to make that deadline. If they don't, it makes no sense to bring that person here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yeah. Okay. 17th will be plenary; 18th we are sitting definitely. Yeah. But don't give me that face, Madam Chuqing, we are sitting on the 18th. Let's bring the witness in and get going.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: We can begin, Your Honour. Unfortunately there's a --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: There's another hitch.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: A technical problem with the Sanction.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: It looked like it from the very word go. Is the cabinet door outside locked where the equipment is? Can someone check, please. This room in the corridor here where all the equipment is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Good morning to you, Mr. Brown. Welcome back. You're going to continue giving evidence on the basis of the same solemn declaration that you made yesterday. So please take a seat, and Mr. Nicholls will proceed. Is the technical fault going to stop? We can proceed, Ms. Gustin? What's the problem, if I may know? Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: We can start, Your Honours, it's just we don't have hard copies of every single document. I have a B/C/S copy of everything I am going to use, so if necessary, we can put that on the ELMO. And hopefully, this will catch up to us.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We try. Anyway, let's start cracking and then we'll see.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Brown.

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Nicholls.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: For your information, I have been asked this morning when both of us are reading, we read a little bit slower if we read from any documents. And for your information, we're going to try to finish by 11.30 if possible. I just want to, if we can, tie up what we were talking about yesterday which within the context of common features of military operations was the series of weapons deadlines. And let me just try to take us up to where we were yesterday. We talked first about the Subotic mobilisation order of the 16th of April and the related 4th of May ARK National Defence council instruction which referenced the Subotic order which first set the deadline of 11th of May at 3.00 p.m., 1500 hours. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: The next item we talked about was the 8th of May, 1992, ARK Crisis Staff conclusion which re-emphasised the 11th of May deadline. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: We then talked about the 11th of May ARK Crisis Staff conclusion which extended the deadline to the 14th of May and raised the language in a sense at this point now stating that severe sanctions shall be taken against those who disobey that proclamation?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: On the 14th of May, the ARK Crisis Staff, and you state in your report, then switched to proactive measures for disarmament. Can you briefly explain what you meant by that. We are now on page 65, paragraph 2.15.

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: The quote on page 65 and 66 from the ARK Crisis Staff decision of the 14th of May stated that: "The Security Services Centre of the Autonomous Region of Krajina shall consistently carry out the decision of the Crisis Staff of the Autonomous Region of Krajina on disarming of paramilitary units and individuals who are illegally in possession of weapons and ammunition." In essence, requesting that the Security Services Centre take action in regard to this.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And then yesterday, we looked at the 14th of May Security Services Centre disarmament order, that's P195, which resulted from that ARK 14th of May meeting.

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Is it possible for me just to refresh myself with that document?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Yes. That is the document cited in footnote 269, I believe. CSB Banja Luka instruction of 14th of May.

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. This document tasks the various chiefs of public security stations to make concrete plans for the seizure of illegally owned weapons and ammunition and explosives. It is dated the 14th of May, which is the same day as the ARK Crisis Staff decision, although I just draw your attention to the fact that in the first paragraph, it actually references earlier decisions rather than that 14th of May decision. But in essence, it is requesting that the various MUP or police chiefs to make concrete plans for the illegal or the seizure of illegally owned weapons and ammunitions, which would seem to be in line with that 14th of May ARK decision.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you for that clarification. One moment, please. All right. One of the documents I planned to show you - we can't put it up on the screen right now, so we'll just refer to it - is the document you footnote in footnote 267.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: For your information, Your Honours, that has been previously exhibited as P631. It's the 12th of May 5th corps command combat report.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: You cite this, do you not, as an example of the deadlines being referenced and disseminated in 5th corps military documents?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. This particular daily combat report is dated the 12th of May, so it's the day after the 11th of May and when the initial deadline was meant to be or was listed for 1500 hours. And it makes reference: "Upon the request of citizens and parties, the Serbian Republic Krajina war staff has extended the deadline for the handover of weapons from 11 May to 14 May," indicating that the corps were aware of these deadlines in some detail and were passing that information on or they viewed it as important enough to put it in a daily combat report and were passing that information up to their higher command headquarters.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you. And we're just about done with this area. We also looked at yesterday the document cited in footnote 389. That was the undated order by Mr. Anicic, commander of the Sanski Most Serbian Territorial Defence. And I believe you selected that document as an example of the way that these disarmament operations in practice were carried out jointly with the involvement of the military and police forces, as well as TO, VRS, and police forces.

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I believe that would indicate this.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And just for the record, that is the process which you talk about in paragraph 2.18 of your report. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And again, would you characterise the process which we see in that Anicic order as representative of the sort of general pattern of disarmament, obviously with differences in the different municipalities?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I think there are a number of documentary references in other municipalities that would appear to echo this type of activity highlighted in the Sanski Most TO instruction.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you. If we could go now to page 88 of your report, could you tell us just very briefly what this section is about, retaliatory actions and killings of non-Serbs. We won't go through all the documents you reference here, but I'd like you to explain why you put this in as part of the general pattern of municipality attacks that we see.

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I primarily put it in because there were a number of references in the military documents, in the Krajina Corps collection, military documents themselves that talked about retaliatory action and killings. They made reference in some cases to specific instances of killings. They made a number of general references to the issue of retaliatory actions and killings. And there were some references as well from the corps passing down instructions that indicated that this type of activity was to be prevented. So I put it in because the documents themselves made reference to it.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And in paragraph 2.80 of your report, which is on page 89, you've listed representative examples of these types of killings where they occurred in different municipalities, such as Bosanski Gradiska, Celinac, the Keraterm camp, Manjaca, Sanski Most, and so on.

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I tried as best I could to look at the individual case that is I saw, and those were some of them that were flagged up in the various reports of the corps. And I also made the references to some of the general comments on killings and retaliatory action which I flagged up in the sections -- this section and the subsequent sections.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Just as an example, I'd like to show the document cited in footnote 405. This has not been previously exhibited, and I'd like to make it an exhibit. It will be P2424. I can put my copy on the ELMO if necessary.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Still the technical hitch hasn't been solved as yet?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Apparently not, Your Honour. So I will have to operate without the document. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: This is a 1st Krajina Corps regular combat report dated the 22nd of August. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is, and it is going to the main staff of the VRS.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Can you just briefly tell us why you selected this one as an example. I think it's obvious, actually. You don't need to answer that. Just go to the highlighted portion where this document deals with killings which the corps was made aware of.

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Paragraph 3, situation on the ground. In the second part of that paragraph makes note: "A massacre against civilians, Muslim men, was committed on the 21st of August between 1830 and 1900 hours. It was committed by a group of policemen escorting a convoy of refugees to Travnik. The massacre took place at Koricanke Stijene in the canyon of Ilomska river at Mount Vlasic. About 100 people were killed in various ways and left in the canyon."

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you. I'm done with that exhibit. Just for completeness, footnote 406, the next footnote in your report, we won't put the document on the screen.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: That is P2302, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: It has been exhibited. It's another report dealing with this incident -- no, I'm sorry. Strike that. That is another example of a different massacre which you selected showing -- reporting up through the chain of command of the corps. This one, however, dealing with an incident in Kotor Varos at the Vecici village?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. This was on the 4th of November in relation to the activity in Vecici, which was an area that the Serb authorities had not got under control at that time. And during this period, there were negotiations in an attempt to resolve that area, and there were some disagreements between how that should be resolved, whether weapons should be handed over or whether they should be allowed to leave and just move from the territory. It appears that whilst those negotiations were ongoing, the men from that area of Vecici attempted to leave and break out, and this daily combat report notes that they were or a significant number were captured. And it states in this daily combat report which again was sent to the VRS main staff headquarters: "In the area of Kotor Varos, there was a clash between members of Muslim forces and our units. Because of the refusal to negotiate on the moving out of the area of the Vecici area, about 40 Green Beret members were killed and about 200 were captured. A brutal massacre of the captured members of the Green Berets started because of the killing of one soldier of the Kotor Varos light infantry brigade and the burning of wounded soldiers on the Gola Planina in Jajce." Subsequently daily combat reports in the following days couched this incident or the deaths as combat casualties rather than in particular reference to a massacre of captured prisoners.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you. I'd like to move on to a different section of your report. This begins on page 97. The section of your report entitled: The Rounding of Population, Transfer to Camps, and Detention Centres. Now, is this again, this section of the report, a feature which you would characterise as one of the common features of the military operations in the Krajina in 1992 which you studied?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it was. Certainly in the municipalities where the documentary evidence was reasonably substantial and in the military reports as well, it would seem to be, as I've articulated, that after many of the attacks, a significant number of people were taken and placed in various detention centres, initially in those municipalities, and then transferred to a larger Detention Centre.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: All right. I'd like to look at one of the documents you've selected as representative in this section. That is footnote 449. It has been previously exhibited as P657. We can't put it on the screen. This is a 2nd of June 1st Krajina Corps command regular combat report to the army main staff. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is. It's another standard daily combat report from the corps to the main staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Perhaps we could put your version on the ELMO, and you can take my version because my version has handwriting on it.

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can probably read it the ELMO.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: All right. This essentially goes to the point of the rounding up or gathering of the population. If you could just take us to the important points in this document, which I think are mostly in paragraphs 2 and 3.

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. This simply highlights that the corps were aware that significant numbers, in this case, 900, had been captured in the area of fight around Kljuc. Makes mention that some 400 rifles had been seized during the process. There are a couple of other issues which also deal with the issues we were talking about yesterday in relation to the movement out of the population and weapon deadlines. And paragraph 2, in relation to Lisina village which was a village in Prnjavor municipality, Muslim extremists -- because they had failed to hand in their weapons, the Muslim population of the area of Lisina village had been expelled. Also in paragraph 3 it notes that in the wider area of Sanski Most, Prijedor, and Kljuc, they are under the control of our units and mopping up in the area is underway. Paragraph 8 of the document also makes reference to the disarming issue again. Just again referring to disarming of Muslim extremists paramilitary formations, and that that was continuing.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you. I'm done with that document. Also, we don't need to go through the document, but in footnote 451, you cite the report for the Bosanski Novi public security station. That is -- has been numbered 2423. That's another good example of what occurred. That's why you cited that. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That is a very detailed report making reference to this very issue, that significant numbers were taken to detention centres. And in fact, the three documents that comprise this consolidated report all deal with this issue to some degree, highlighting a number of the detention centres that were established and that both through police and military action, that significant numbers were taken to those detention centres.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you. Similarly, we don't need to put it on the ELMO, but footnote 452, you cited a quote from that document which is P680, Your Honours, which just states clearly that on the 25th of May, the "disarming" in Sanski Most was followed by military action against the downtown neighbourhood of Mahala which resulted in the capture of 2.000 civilians, but no significant amount of weapons have been found because they had been concealed earlier. And that is a Sanski Most report on the activities of the Sanski Most SJB dated 15 of June, 1992. That's just another example. Correct?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. And the issue of the date here is also important. It says the 25th, and the Sanski Most Territorial Defence document is the 26th. The daily combat reports of the corps around that period also make reference to operations going on in that municipality. But in relation to the corps, yes, it makes mention of 2.000 civilians being captured.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: We don't need to go through this document because the Chamber has seen it several times, but the document you note in footnote 460, that is the document from the Sanski Most Crisis Staff meeting dated 4th of June, 1992, which deals with the categorisation of prisoners and their selection for deportation to Manjaca camp. The persons listed as taking part in that process are Mirko Vrucinic, who was the chief of police; Nedeljko Racava [phoen]; and Colonel Anicic. We saw his report earlier. Can you just comment on whether this categorisation process was unique to Sanski Most or whether you found evidence of this elsewhere, and also whether this type of selection as to who was to go to camps in other municipalities also involved civilian, police, and military personnel? Sorry, that was a long question.

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I made reference to this in the Stakic testimony. I saw evidence Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. of that in Prijedor from documentation. Again, in Prijedor Municipality, documentation indicated an involvement of military officials and police officials in the categorisation process or -- and selection process. The Sanski Most document that you refer to also includes a reference to the assistant commander for security at the 1st Krajina Corps who was to be contacted also in relation to this categorisation or selection process.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, this document in footnote 460, for the record, is P661.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you. I wonder if we could have a call to the technician, if anybody can make that and see if anybody can again come out and try to help us get this running.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: That's what we have, too, P661.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Moving ahead, I think this is an important paragraph. You've already started talking about this, Mr. Brown. 2.106, on page 100, we don't have time probably for you to give the longest answer you'd like to that. But can you just tell us whether you stand by that statement or have any changes to make to it and if you have anything to add.

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I stand by the statement. I think the documentation indicates a significant degree of cooperation and coordination between the military and the police, including in camps that they themselves did not run.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you. If we could go to page 105 of your report, you are talking in paragraph 2.120 about some of the problems or bad conditions that prisoners in Manjaca camp suffered. There has been a lot of testimony about that, so we won't talk about the actual conditions. But can you talk about the document you cite in 493, footnote 493, that is P394. That is a 1st Krajina Corps command report on the visit by the International Red Cross to Manjaca prisoner of war camp, 16th of July, 1992, signed by Colonel Vukelic. Can you just explain why you included this section in your report.

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was a reasonable amount of material in relation to Manjaca camp in the 1st Krajina Corps documents. That's probably unsurprising seeing as they were running the facility. But this document in particular stood out, and in essence, was the 1st Krajina Corps's report on the ICRC visit to the camp and their perspective of what they viewed from that visit. It was sent to General Talic and was -- summarised not only the visit, but also the views as articulated to the Krajina Corps, the views of the ICRC in relation to the camp. The document just for interest states at the beginning: "At the urging of the Banja Luka-based International Red Cross from Geneva, and in keeping with the agreement sign on the 13th of July, 1992, by Mr. D. Kalinic from the government of the Serbian Republic of BH, a visit to the prisoner of war camp in Manjaca was granted." This is the same Mr. Kalinic who we discussed yesterday at the 16th assembly session. The corps then discuss the ICRC visit. They arrived. But clearly broke off talks with the military. And in it, in this document, it articulates why the ICRC themselves stated that they broke talks off, and they said amongst other things, they hadn't been allowed to meet with prisoners, for prisoners, they made observations about the quantities of food, loss of weight of the prisoners, the risk of an epidemic breaking out. They demanded the release of some 19 prisoners on account of the state of their health. And they used the words in the document "brought out accusations that the treatment of prisoners and claimed to have seen fresh traces of blood." The document states that -- gives the impression that the ICRC hadn't come with, if you like, a proper assignment and that they had actually had some ulterior motive and states in the paragraph the general impression is that the ICRC representatives came on an assignment. And there's references at the end: "As we have discovered that their intentions are not based on goodwill, we suggest that they continue to be watched closely, that we permit them to visit more often but decline hospitality when the opportunity arises." This document for me is indicative that the ICRC view the camp as being -- the conditions being poor within the camp, but that the Krajina Corps are not willing to accept that in view that the ICRC as coming on in for some ulterior purpose and that if necessary, they should decline further access if required.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you. Could we go to page 107 of your report now, paragraph 2.127. And in relation to this section, I'll ask you whether you found documentary evidence in the 1st Krajina Corps collection which showed whether the 1st Krajina Corps was aware that civilians, in other words, persons who had not committed a crime or were not engaged in armed combat, were held in Manjaca camp?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, there is documentation to that effect.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: If we're working now, could we have footnote 509, please. That is P1314, Your Honours, 1st Krajina Corps command letter, I suppose, 6th of August, 1992, to the Prijedor SMB. Now, I think this is fairly self-explanatory why you selected this --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Frankly, I don't know -- I can't fathom why you're asking a question on it. Because if you read those four lines, that's what it says, and that's footnote 509. And we have seen this document before.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: My only point, Your Honour, is that it shows again this communication between the prisoners, not just the military, whether they are talking to the Prijedor authorities saying that some action needs to be taken.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And just also, Mr. Brown, Manjaca camp would have been in operation for a couple of months. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I would draw attention also to of course the second-last section which states that: "Having been attacked in the media, that this was justification enough or sufficient reason enough to carry out the selection." Having looked at this document, there is a difference in the typeface of the address block. It says to Prijedor SMB. And then the last line also says "please forward to Omarska".

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: For the record, you're talking about the B/C/S original.

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: The B/C/S original, yes. But in the body of the text it makes mention to Sanski Most. My assessment of this is that this document was designed for a number of municipalities and quite possibly the assistant commander of security drafted it up initially for Sanski Most and simply took off the address block rather than having is to rewrite or retype the document and sent this version to Prijedor. And I believe this version was actually seized in Prijedor by the Office of the Prosecutor. So it may well have been not just disseminated to Prijedor, but to other SMBs from where prisoners in Manjaca came from.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you very much. I'd like to just look at another document. This has not been exhibited. That is the document cited in footnote 511, a 3rd of September 1st Krajina Corps command document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And that would be P2425.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: We're on the same topic here, Mr. Brown. I think if you could comment on this, the relevant portions are on page 3 and 4, further talking about the problem of having citizens for which there is no evidence that they committed any type of criminal activity being detained. If we look at the bottom of page 3.

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. This is a fairly detailed report, again summarising activity in the corps. And it does state on page 3: "Certain tensions are still present in the Kotor Varos, Kljuc, Sanski Most, and Prijedor areas because of a large number of arrested citizens for whom there's no evidence or criminal reports that they participated in the armed rebellion." There are -- there are a number of other key sections of this document which we can cover later or cover now.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Why don't we do it now if there's something you'd like to point Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. out from this document, we should do while we're here.

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: In relation to visits to the camps, there's a comment at the top of the section about the visit of Tadeusz Mazowiecki who is a UN Special Rapporteur who visited a number of camps in Bosnia, and also visited -- or attempted to visit Manjaca camp. And it makes comments more generally about the visits at this time or in the previous month of the international community and the press being aware within the international community of camps. And on page 2, it states: "The intolerant attitude of the international community towards the Serb's position in BH is causing extreme distrust of their goodwill. In this period, there was a great interest in the visits to LRZs," which I believe are detention camps. "With euphoria, the dominant feeling, interest in the sick and difficult cases and attempts to show the world, public, the unbearable condition in these camps. These and especially their negative portrayal of the situation has increased antagonism of soldiers towards these international institutions. We are confronted with the problems of having to refuse their visits to many checkpoints because of this. The most evident example was the calculated, tactless, and unannounced visit by Mr. Tadeusz Mazowiecki the Special Rapporteur. Although the majority of foreign journalists portrayed the situation very realistically, both on the battlefield and in the LRZs controlled by us, some journalists especially from Canada used skillfull fabrications to try to blame the Serbs and the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia for the crisis." There's another reference further down on this document until to the ICRC and the view of the Krajina Corps at this time towards the ICRC. "The ICRC's approach to distributing humanitarian aid is having a very detrimental effect on morale of soldiers and units. This aid is mostly distributed to prisoners of war, Muslims, Croats, and crisis areas. Not a single case has been registered that aid was given to threaten Serbs whose lives are becoming increasingly hard because of the participation of soldiers on the front, electricity shortages, disrupted distribution of supplies, and the overall blockade." There's a reference in paragraph 2. I'd like to draw your attention to a note of the overall political and security situation August 1992 was characterised by the following: "The activities of several paramilitary governments and armed formations, increased extremism towards the Muslim and Croat population, continued efforts to place the organs of authorities and the MUP above military formations and the army, RIK," which I believe is command and control system. And it states: "For these reasons the 1st Krajina Corps commander held a meeting with all unit commanders and municipal presidents at which he pointed to the problem of existence of para-governments and paramilitaries and the need to overcome this crisis in view of the objectives of the war we are waging at the present time. This was followed by a certain relaxation of tensions and activities directed at overcoming the crisis and help the legal functioning of the Serbian republic." This again cuts to what we were discussing yesterday in relation to it wasn't a seamless relationship, and there were undoubtedly some difficulties, but the methods in which were implied to try and relax those issues. There is also a reference in this document to the massacre we discussed in relation to Mount Vlasic on page 3 and pages 4, states: "The CSB especially interest Prijedor is not contributing to this approach. Prijedor headed by Stevo Drljaca" - they got the name slightly wrong - "who led a convoy of people who wanted to leave the crisis area, they committed a massacre in the Skender Vakuf area of over 150 men who wanted to leave the territory of the Krajina Autonomous Region. This action caused indignation not only among citizens but also among the 1st Krajina Corps soldiers. This dark stain which was created did not have support, but it is very fortunate that the international community did not find out about it in more detail." There are some other issues which we discussed yesterday in relation to some of the topics of the government relationship and functioning of the courts that are also referenced in this document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Nicholls.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Brown. And you have a section in the next paragraph 2.130 of your report, still on page 108. We've seen that in August, the 1st Krajina Corps was acutely aware that citizens were being held at Manjaca camp. What evidence did you find that citizens were released from Manjaca camp because they should not have been there and when did that take place?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: The documents indicated that it wasn't until November that there was a release, and that was relatively limited in terms of the numbers of prisoners who were there. And it wasn't until December 1992 when the camp closed that the majority of the prisoners were released.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And according to the documentation you've found, how were these people released? You cite it well in your report, but I take it that it wasn't an, we apologise for holding you for so long. You're free to go back to your municipality you came from. That's not what occurred is it?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. They were taken on buses and taken to Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Do you connect that in any way to the issue of resettlement which we were talking about quite a lot yesterday.

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do. I do. I think I've argued in the report that the issue of detention camps I don't think can be separated from that overall objective of resettlement.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And I think paragraph 2.133 in your report on page 109, you explain that position. And the last sentence of that paragraph on page 110 states: "These camps were in essence a component in the policy of separation in which the military participated." That's correct, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Could you just briefly talk about the other evidence you saw in compiling your report of civilian and police cooperation or coordination in the topic of camps in general in addition to just bringing people to the camps which we've already talked about and the selection of those who went to the camps, because you do talk about a couple other topics in that paragraph. I'm referring to the establishment of the camps and the transfer of prisoners between camps.

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I think the whole process, the initial capture, movement to initial detention centres, the selection process, transfer on to established detention centres, security issues in relation to detention centres, and the movement out and transfer out of people from those detention centres, often included both military, civilian, and police involvement.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Your Honours, I don't know if I said it, but I'd like to say it for the record, the document cited in footnote 518, it's the 1st Krajina Corps command regular army report which talks about prisoners being released from Manjaca camp, a thousand of them being escorted out of the territory of the RS. Your Honours, that is P441, for your reference. I don't think we need to go through the whole document.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I notice also, Mr. Nicholls, that 516 is 441, too.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Footnote 516.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: In our spreadsheet, 518 is unmarked as an exhibit. And you're telling us it's 441, P441. But I notice that footnote 516 refers to Exhibit P441, which is different.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I may have made a mistake, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Which will certainly not be the first one or the last.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Sorry, Your Honour. I think I would like to put 518 -- it needs an exhibit number. If we can put that up, and I will enter that as --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We will give it 2426.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Yes. In that case, I'd just ask Mr. Brown to look at it.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: If you can tell us whether that stands for the proposition we were talking about, prisoners once they were released from Manjaca camp were not released to their homes but were escorted out of the territory of the RS.

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, also in this section, it states that 413 prisoners are to remain and be used for exchange, presumably prisoner exchange, with Serbs that were being held in other areas.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, the next section of your report, still on page 110, is something we've talked about all along, the removal of the non-Serb population from towns and villages. I'd like to just look at a couple documents which you've selected to illustrate this process. The first one is one of the documents listed in footnote 522. There are a couple documents in there. This is a 1 KK, 13th of August, 1992, regular combat report to the main staff. Hopefully it will come up in a minute. This is another document authored by Colonel Vukelic.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: This will be P2427, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Well, it will come up in a minute, but before it does, can you -- this is fairly self-evident, but explain why you selected this document for this section of your report.

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. This was another document that made reference to the fact that a large number of Muslims and Croats were moving out of the territory. The military documents used different words, different times, but this was one that I choose as a footnote. And it states in paragraph 3 on the situation in the territory: "In the area of Prijedor in the Sana valley, no new extremist or rebel groups were detected, and there's a growing number of requests for an organised moving out of Muslims and Croats from the entire area of the Autonomous Region of Krajina."

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you. The next document I'd like you to look at in this regard, similar, it's also in footnote 522. This has been exhibited as P421, Your Honours. This is the 1st Krajina Corps command 6 September 1992 regular combat report to the main staff. And could you please just comment on your selection of this particular document to illustrate the removal of the non-Serb population.

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, again, this is a document a little bit later. It states: "attacks on all areas of the Serb Republic and Republic of Serbian Krajina may be launched very soon, especially after the exodus of the majority of the Croatian population and a part of the Muslim population from Banja Luka and other towns." This is just another example. This time it's called an exodus, but it's another example in the military documents, contemporary military documents, of their awareness that a significant number of Croats and Muslims were leaving the Autonomous Region of Krajina. And in the report, I've listed other references that make note of those. They do use different phrases and different words, but there are a reasonable number of references in the Krajina documents or military documents especially to this effect.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Now, if we go to paragraph 2.136 of your report, it's on page 111, you discuss there evidence again of cooperation or coordination between military, civilian, and police authorities, or at least their awareness of this issue of the movement out of the population and resettlement and active cooperation between these bodies. Can you just talk about how -- a little bit about how you arrived at that conclusion?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Could you reference the page again, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Page 111, top of the page 2.136. Take your time to read that section and refresh your memory.

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think in the chapter itself, I've referenced a number of footnotes that would indicate this issue that there was cooperation between military and civilian authorities that make reference to the knowledge and the movement out of the population. In a number of Crisis Staff minutes, they discuss this. It's referenced in military documents. And I think a lot of the footnotes in this chapter make -- attest to that.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you. If we look at footnote 539, that's Exhibit P1608, Your Honours. This is an excerpt of minutes from the Kotor Varos war presidency of the 14th of July, 1992. The reference is on page 113 of the report, in paragraph 2.142. I think this goes to what we have been talking about. Can you just explain why you introduced this document into your report.

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. It's a Crisis Staff meeting at which there was military representatives and civilian representatives. And item 2 on the agenda makes reference to activities relating to the moving out of the population failed to meet expectation. This task must be dealt with in a much more organised fashion, and an agency has to be established to handle these matters. This is one small example at Kotor Varos municipality whereby this issue of removal is being discussed and action is being suggested in the moving out of the population. It's by no means the only example, I think, in my references.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you. Similarly, if we go to another document you referenced, that is footnote 563, this appears on page 118 of your report. This is a 1st Krajina Corps command 10th of July, 1992, combat report to the main staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Your Honours, this has been previously exhibited as 1469.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: We just looked at a Crisis Staff document from Kotor Varos. Could you look at -- explain why you included this 1 KK report which talks about similar issues.

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, this again just indicates what we discussed yesterday and this morning, that the corps were acutely aware of the movement out of the territory of non-Serbs, and it states that: "Muslim organisation in Kotor Varos is initiating negotiations on the modes of migration from these areas." This time it's called migration. And it also makes note that there have been people moving away in other areas, but in Banja Luka there are still some difficulties because the authorities are not sufficiently organised in implementing this model for they call the removal of the enemy. So it's just an interesting reference in terms of the language used and their knowledge that people are leaving, non-Serbs are leaving the territory.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you. The next and last document I'd like to look at on this issue appears in footnote 573 which -- actually the reference begins on page 119 of your report, paragraph 2.158.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Your Honours, this has previously been exhibited as P1059.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: It's a fairly detailed report of events in Kljuc. It's written in -- it's dated 16th of February, 1993, but refers back in a sort of summary of activities during the combat period in May. Could you please explain to us what this report is and the areas you find most significant. You can take your time to find and look at the report.

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: This document, I think, is useful in -- to some degree showing us a vignette some of the issues I discussed yesterday and today. It's a document written in February 1993, but clearly referring back to activities in the previous months in Kljuc municipality. And it's a document that was written after a meeting that had been held apparently on the 3rd of February, 1993, involving many of the significant representatives in Kljuc municipality, civilian representatives, police representatives, as well as the commander of the 17th Brigade, Colonel Drago Samardzija. The 17th Brigade had been formed out of a brigade that was under General Talic's command, the 1st Partisan Brigade, which was actually a component of the 30th Brigade. And in this meeting, they are clearly discussing many issues in relation to Kljuc Municipality. And it appears that as a result of this meeting, the assistant commander for civilian affairs of the 17th Brigade toured the area of Kljuc, either was asked to write a report on the situation, and this appears to be that report. And in it, he writes about the activities that had occurred in Kljuc in essence from May 1992 onwards, and he makes a number of important comments. I draw your attention to page 2 which talks about the onset of the war in the Kljuc area. And if I run through some of the comments he makes, he states: "As I have already pointed out, the war was imposed on us by our centuries-old enemies who hated and still hate everything Serbian. In this century, they have committed three acts of genocide against us. The fight against Ustasha villains commenced on the 27th of May, 1992, in the territory of the Velagici local commune and soon spilled over to the area north of Kljuc. This happened in the predominantly Muslim areas. Indeed, the Serbian army, police, and Serbian people crushed and routed genocide-prone Ustashas in one fell swoop and cleansed the remaining Ustashas from the Kljuc municipality. By this act, the Serbian people made a clean break once and for all with the centuries-old enemy." I think this particular section has some importance both in terms of the language used and the reason he puts forward as why the activity -- combat activity occurred. But I draw your attention to his reference to the date, 27th of May, and my references in footnote 274 which relate to disarmament issues and decrees that were articulated in Kljuc Municipality. Again, cutting back to what I discussed yesterday about the importance from the documents of this issue of disarmament as being the -- an important feature in municipalities and linking to the attacks that occurred in those municipalities. He then goes on to talk about individuals and large groups who began illegally appropriating Muslim property and Muslim villages and hamlets during combat actions and also later on after combat actions had ceased. He made reference that this was done by military personnel, members of the police, and local Serbs, and this problem had been as he called, spread like an epidemic, and that moveable and immoveable property had been stolen from areas, Muslim and Croat areas, in the municipality. He makes reference that in order to stop this type of activity, that the municipality pass a decree saying that moveable and immoveable property in areas that had been Muslim and Croat was to become the property of the state. Now, that -- although he doesn't reference it in this document, I've referenced a document in my report in relation to this issue of appropriating for state use the moveable and immoveable property from those who had left or who had been forced to leave or who had been taken prisoner. And in my report, I draw certainly from the military's perspective this distinction that in many ways there was, from a military and General Talic's comments, documents talking about we should stamp down on looting of moveable and immoveable property, that individuals were getting wealthy on the back of this, but that there was a mechanism by which moveable and immovable property was to be appropriated for the state use and for the benefit of the RS authorities. And that was not challenged by the military. But where they felt uneasy about the issue of looting, that it was individuals in essence taking property rather than it being used for the benefits of the state. And I believe that this document also makes reference to that, too. On page 4, the document talks about in detail the issue of departure of Muslims from the period of May 1992. And in it, he lists a number of the communes and areas within Kljuc Municipality which I've referenced in my report also. And he lists the number of residents who were in the municipality or the commune prior to the combat action and how many were left. And it's very clear that in those communes which are predominantly Muslim, that most of the communes are -- there are very few people left in them. And this document really for me is important in highlighting a knowledge that that was the state of play in this particular municipality.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And it also, does it not, you read through this section, but I think it's important, on page 2, the language about how the Serb people routed this century-old enemy and cleansed the area. The credit in that paragraph is given, is it not, not just to the military but to the military, the police, and the Serbian people acting together?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, very much. And in terms of the language, it's a very stark language in comparison to the type of language that was being used earlier in JNA and military reports at the end of 1991 and early 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: We talked about that yesterday as well.

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Just before we move on to the final area I want to talk about, paragraph -- in paragraph 2.160, we won't go through it all, I think that's an important section of your report. In that case, you are summarising some of the similar issues as they are referenced in SJB or CSB reports relating to the movement out of the population during this period.

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Those reports also indicate figures and numbers of people who have left in those municipalities that I've quoted.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Your Honours, I'm up to the last section. I'll definitely finish on schedule. I don't think I can finish it in 5 or 6 minutes, so I wonder if we could take a short break now early, and I'll finish right after we come back.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: How much time do you require more or less?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I think about 15, 20 minutes. Maybe less.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I don't know. I was going to suggest, if it is okay with everyone obviously because I haven't consulted everyone, if we could have a very short break so that they change the tapes, say 5 minutes or so, and then we go on for the next 15 minutes, 20 minutes, and then we finish. All right, so we'll have a 20-minute break. Thank you. Incidentally, before we leave the courtroom, Mr. Ackerman, when you come to the cross-examination of this witness, and Mr. Treanor, you are being authorised as from now to bring forward and sit by your side an expert of your own if you want who would be able to assist you in your cross-examination to secure a more efficient cross-examination. I know from experience that when it comes to cross-examine an expert witness, having by your side your own expert witness, your own expert helps you very much in conducting a proper cross-examination. That would apply, of course, to the Prosecution, too, if and when Mr. Ackerman brings forward his own expert witnesses.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: You mean, Your Honours, that the expert can literally pass questions to Mr. Ackerman?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: What I mean is Mr. Ackerman may have sitting next to him say a military expert of his own. And -- because what happens is you put a question, you don't always anticipate the answer. Sometimes you get an answer, and if you're not an expert yourself on the matter, you don't know how to follow up. And if you have your expert sitting next to you, he will direct you to having a proper, efficient cross-examination. But this is in case I forget, so I'm telling you now. 20-minute break. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Nicholls. Wait until the accused takes his -- oh, no. This is the Stakic. Could Ms. Gustin remind me what exhibit number we gave to the Stakic transcript?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: 2415. Thank you. Let's proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours. Apparently we're again having a problem with the Sanction, so I may just use the ELMO. There are a couple of documents I wish to enter, new exhibits.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Mr. Brown, the last section of your report I want to cover is that contained in pages 157 through 161 entitled: "Cooperation with the FRY." Can you go to that section of your report, please.

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I have it here.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Now, in this section you talk about essentially three types of cooperation, that of logistic supply, financial and personnel issues, and communication, radio, and technical reconnaissance. Could you please just briefly give us a definition or just a shorthand explanation of what those three types of assistance entail when you use those terms, in your report, what do they go to?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, logistic supply obviously is anything that can keep a military functioning and covers a wide array of topics, from ammunition, fuel, medical, anything that can keep the army going. Finance and personnel issue clearly is fairly self-explanatory. And communication and radio technical reconnaissance relates to communication issues in terms of ensuring information can flow between units and formations. So it covers those areas.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: All right. Speaking -- well, you begin in 2.253, that paragraph on page 157, just to be clear, that after the establishment of the VRS in May, there continued to be close links with the -- you say, between the VRS and the VJ after that transition. Correct?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I initially in the report, when I was looking at the issue of the 16th assembly session and relations to the objectives and looking into the issue of, to coin a phrase, all Serbs in one state, wanted to look into the military documentation to see what evidence there may be in relation to this link between the VRS and VJ. And that was the reason I began looking at the documentation for that.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: All right. In paragraph 2.255 on the same page, you talk about a plan to supply logistics report which was named "IZVOR" or "Source." And that included ammunition and other material. Could we please look at your footnote 764, that's a VRS main staff instruction dated 12th September, 1992. And that will be P2428. And we need to put that on the ELMO, I'm afraid. I will put my copy up. It has got some highlighting on it. May I ask you to briefly explain to us what that document tells you and why you selected it for this topic of logistic supply.

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: This document dated 12th September comes from the assistant commander for logistics at the main staff, Major-General Djordje Djukic. And he was writing back to the 1st Krajina Corps, to General Talic personally in relation to a correspondence that had apparently taken place the previous day. And the document makes reference to this plan, IZVOR. And it states: "Following the agreement with the general staff of the Federal Republic of Yugoslav army, we have been granted the required amount of ammunition. In keeping with the IZVOR Source plan, the 14th logistics base has begun taking the ammunition and has so far taken over 225 tonnes. The takeover of the remaining 220 tonnes follows." He then talks about this logistics base having to supply both the 1st and 2nd Krajina Corps and its own logistic commands, and to check whether any surplus ammunition they don't need from presumably this delivered ammunition. It states: "The situation with ammunition supply is very difficult since all ammunition factories are either closed or working at minimum capacity. The SRJ reserves are limited. We have undertaken measures to procure raw material for the production of higher calibre ammunition. According to the agreement reached, the base and the corps are also allowed to procure ammunition and fuel in the SRJ provided that the base or corps representatives go to the base in Pancevo to discuss the amounts and the loading point. At present this applies to the agreement under the IZVOR plan, and for later cases you will receive further instructions on what to do and how to proceed." The date is of some significance in that it comes only a month or two, or a few months after the corridor was established, the corridor operation started in the end of June. A corridor link was established very swiftly, within a week or two, and then there were operations to widen that corridor through July and August. So this comes to all intents and purposes on the back of the success of operation corridor and clearly is a plan for the provision of ammunition between the SRJ and the VRS.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you. I'm done with that document. In addition to ammunition, you talk about other supplies which were provided. If we look at your footnote 770 on page 158.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Your Honours, that is part of a larger document which has previously been exhibited as P2419.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: You have selected a chart from a VRS main staff document entitled "Analysis of the Combat Readiness of the Army of the Republika Srpska in 1992." The document, the analysis, dated April 1993. Unfortunately, because of the photocopy, this is a bit difficult to read, but could you explain what this diagram represents in terms of the logistic support we have been talking about.

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is the document we discussed very briefly yesterday which was a very large document in relation to many aspects of the VRS. And in the section that deals with logistics, this chart is apparent, and the bottom chart is a graphic representation of the ammunition received according to the IZVOR and Pretis plans. The darker blocks on the chart, and in fact, the original is easier to read than the translation, the darker blocks indicate the tonnage of ammunition that was received from the SRJ in relation to the IZVOR plan. And from this chart, it appears that 7.451 tonnes of ammunition had been received in accordance with this plan.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you. And in the following paragraphs, 2.256, you talk about other references to logistic supply which we won't go through all of them in detail. I would like to look at one of them which has not yet been made an exhibit. That is footnote 775. This is a 1st Krajina Corps command regular combat report to the main staff from 6 December, 1992. And this, again, talks about some logistic support being provided, I believe, in the form of repairs or services. Could you explain that, please.

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. In section 6 dealing with logistic support, it makes reference to the fact that 3.000 82-millimetre shells had come back from repairs in the SRJ.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you. And I think that's fairly self-explanatory. That's P2429, Your Honours, please. The next document I'd like to look at is footnoted as 777 in the same section of your report. This is a 1st Krajina Corps fuel authorisation certificate dated 21st of October, 1992. And this will be P2430, please. Could you --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Nicholls, I can't trace which document we gave the number 2428. Can you help me.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: That was footnote 764, Your Honour, I'm told.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Yes, that's a VRS main staff instruction from 12th September, 1992.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: 2428. I don't quite know whether it went in the transcript. I don't think it did. Let's go on.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, while we're at a short pause, I notice that all the exhibit numbers are going in today with a slash between the numbers. I hope that gets fixed in the final one so that that slash is not there because that makes it difficult to do searches. And just for the court reporter and for the people that are working on transcripts, I'd like to make sure that gets cleared up.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, all right. I've found it now. All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Ackerman. I hadn't noticed that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Footnote 777, I've forgotten now, that was 2430, again fairly self-explanatory, but could you tell us why you selected this one and its significance to you.

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is a blank authorisation certificate, although it is signed by General Talic. It again makes reference to fuel being taken over, which is a logistic issue, in the territory of the FRY. And the important issue is that it's pursuant to an order of the 3rd of August issued by the chief of the general staff of the Yugoslav army for logistics. So again, it indicates a senior level or a high level of authorisation and cooperation to allow you this -- this assistance to occur in relation to fuel.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And Your Honours, I notice that we haven't been able to put this up --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I didn't mean to interrupt Mr. Nicholls, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I was just going to say we could put this on the ELMO because apparently there's a difficulty in retrieving it.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Is it possible that the ERN on that is 03005269 instead of 5296?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: It's 5269 on the --

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Because the footnote indicates 5296.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: That may be an error, if we could put this on the ELMO, we can all be sure this is the document.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think this might be on the errata sheet that I did to the report. I think I did make a mistake in putting the ERN reference.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And actually, between -- in the spreadsheet that we were given, it is 5269. So we need to decide. Anyway, it can be checked easily.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Yes. I'm done with that document, thank you, unless you have any other comment you'd like to make, Mr. Brown.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I don't.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Finally, turning to page 160 of your report, finishing with logistics assistance, the section Financial and Personnel Issues, you begin talking about that in paragraph 2.260. And in that paragraph, you discuss some of the problems facing the VRS at that time in terms of finance, salaries, that type of -- that type of -- those types of problems. You've selected a document in footnote 784 which illustrates how some of this assistance, financial assistance, took place.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: This is VRS -- it's the same document we looked at earlier, Your Honours. P2419. The analysis from April 1993, it's just a different page of that larger document. This is a bit detailed.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Could you explain why you selected this and what the different sections mean in terms of financing of the VRS army.

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I only really selected it to highlight the fact that post-transition between the JNA and the VRS, that Yugoslavia continued to pay the salaries of officers, noncommissioned officers, and soldiers working under contract and workers, civilian workers, who remained in the VRS after this period. And this is a quote -- or there's two references in this combat analysis readiness report to that effect. So there continued to be a component of the VRS paid directly from Belgrade in relation to salaries and payments. That's why I added this quote in.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And we can just see - we don't need to go through it completely in detail - but there were different stages in which the assistance or the problems facing the VRS had different forms.

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. It appears that there was an initial period whereby Belgrade continued to pay. Then the RS authorities financed a component of the army, but that these people who had previously been JNA personnel, officers, NCOs, soldiers, civilians under contract and the like continued to be paid directly from Belgrade. There were some difficulties in terms of payment. General Talic made some comments himself at times, but this document and others indicated that this payment of those people remained from Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you have any other comment you'd like to make on that document or financial and personnel issues?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I think I have made some references and comments in the report itself. I've nothing necessarily to add there.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: That's the end of my direct examination, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, Mr. Nicholls. So that brings us to the end of the first part of your testimony, Mr. Brown. As I explained to you yesterday, you will need to return here at some later point in time. I can't tell you the exact date now. But it's assumed to be either end of August or beginning of October, depends on what Mr. Ackerman and Ms. Korner or Mr. Nicholls decide. Yes, Mr. Ackerman, I see you're standing.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, I can tell you now that it will have to be in October, early in our first sitting in October.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: It's no problem. As I explained, you have -- you are free to bring over your expert to assist you in the cross-examination. That also supplies also when you cross-examine Mr. Treanor. So that's it. Mr. Brown, I don't know how to thank you. You have been extremely helpful.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you for your time, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And you'll be escorted. You are free to communicate with Ms. Korner and Mr. Nicholls on anything barring what you've testified about. All right? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So -- yes, Mr. Nicholls.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'd like to know -- just one second, I'm sorry. I have one point but I need to... Just because I'm not sure, Your Honour, can we go into private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Let's go into private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: at 11.17 a.m., to be reconvened on Monday, the 14th day of July, 2003, at 2.15 p.m. 21 22 23 24 25
